items.citation: [2026] NSWDC 409 (Newlinds SC DCJ, 6 November 2026)
items.significance: An inmate who joined a group knife attack in a cell had his moral culpability substantially reduced by childhood trauma (Bugmy), but deterrence for prison violence still produced 5 years 9 months.
items.document: Cases/Crime/R v Binge [2026] NSWDC 409 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - R v Binge [2026] NSWDC 409 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
**Kohen Binge**, 22, joined a group attack on an inmate in his cell and wounded him with a home-made knife. He pleaded guilty
early to **reckless wounding in company** (s 35(3), maximum 10 years; standard non-parole period 4 years).
items.use_it_for:

| Issue | Held |

items.citation: NSW Law Reform Commission, Report 133 (2012)
items.significance: The Commission found the Bail Act 1978 complex and restrictive, with remand numbers more than trebled in 15 years, and recommended a new Act built on a presumption in favour of release.
items.lead: The Attorney General referred bail law to the Commission on **8 June 2011**. The Commission received 40 submissions, held 19 consultation meetings and reported in **April 2012**, concluding that a new, simplified Bail Act was required (para 0.1).
items.use_it_for:
- **Law reform** done by the book: a documented problem, a reference to a law reform body, consultation, a report, then legislation. Contrast it with the 2014 and 2015 amendments, which followed individual cases.
- **PEARR JAM:** responsiveness (reform responding to evidence), protection of individual rights (the presumption in favour of release), and justice achieved.

sections.What it found about the Bail Act 1978:
- **Complexity.** Amendments had made the Act "difficult to comprehend and operate, even for those with legal expertise" (para 0.9) and NSW had "one of the most convoluted and restrictive bail statutes in Australia" (para 0.10).
- **Offence-based presumptions.** Amendments had removed the presumption in favour of bail for some offences, introduced a presumption against it for others and required "exceptional circumstances" for others again (para 0.10).
- **Remand.** The tightening cut failures to appear but at a significant cost in remand numbers; there was no evidence it reduced crime or offending on bail (para 0.11). Remand prisoner numbers had **more than trebled in 15 years** and the rat…
sections.What it recommended:
- A new Act in plain English.
- A **'justification' model** (a person is released unless detention is justified by five mandatory considerations) rather than the Victorian 'unacceptable risk' model (para 0.32; Rec 10.1, 10.2).
- A **uniform presumption in favour of release**, except on appeal (para 0.27; Rec 8.1).
- Two repeat applications for adults before the bar applies (Rec 19.1).
sections.What Parliament did: The Attorney General, Greg Smith, introduced the Bail Bill on **1 May 2013**: the 1978 Act had been amended by more than 80 other Acts; presumptions applied by offence and "may not reflect the actual seriousness of the alleged offending"; the "key feature" was "a simple unacceptable-risk test". items.citation: Unreported (NSWSC, Harrison J, 23 June 2014)
items.significance: A man accused of murder, whose conviction had been sent for retrial, was granted bail under the 2013 Act with strict conditions; murder no longer carried a presumption against bail.
items.lead: **Mahmoud ('Mick') Hawi**, a former president of the Comanchero Motorcycle Club's Sydney chapter, was convicted by a jury in 2011 of the murder of Anthony Zervas in the Sydney Airport brawl of 22 March 2009. He appealed and the Court of Criminal Appeal divided, so a retrial was ordered.
items.use_it_for:
- **Law reform:** conditions can manage risk (the unacceptable risk test), but publicity drove reform.
- **Enforceability:** the conditions are detailed and enforceable; the surety is an incentive to comply.
items.caution: No neutral citation was verified: cite the decision as reported by the ABC. The earlier Evidence Finder wording gave the year as 2014 only; the date and judge above come from the ABC report.

sections.Held:
- On **23 June 2014** Harrison J granted bail (ABC News, 23 June 2014). Hawi's counsel applied under the new Act, which had commenced about a month earlier: **murder no longer carried a presumption against bail**.
- Justice Harrison accepted that some unacceptable risks existed but could be **"adequately mitigated by the imposition of appropriate conditions"**.
- Conditions: good behaviour; daily reporting to police; a curfew; no contact with Crown witnesses and listed people; no new passport; stay more than one kilometre from any airport or international departure point; a **$700,000 surety**.
- The Crown opposed bail, citing his active membership of the Comanchero club and a risk to witnes…
sections.What followed: Hawi's bail and Fesus's a week earlier were two of the three high-profile decisions that preceded the Premier's review (Brown and Quilter, 2014). Hawi pleaded guilty to manslaughter on 4 September 2014 and was shot dead in 2018.

items.title: Inquest into the death of Roberto Laudisio Curti (NSW Coroner, 14 November 2012)
items.citation: Inquest into the death of Roberto Laudisio Curti, NSW State Coroner's Court, findings 14 November 2012
items.significance: The Coroner found police use of Tasers and force against a 21-year-old student was reckless and excessive; five officers were referred for disciplinary action and the Ombudsman reviewed Taser rules.
items.lead: **Roberto Laudisio Curti**, a 21-year-old Brazilian student, died in the Sydney CBD on 18 March 2012 after a pursuit by police over the theft of two packets of biscuits. He was unarmed and affected by LSD. Officers tasered him repeatedly (including in 'drive stun' mode while he was held on the ground), used capsicum spray and handcuffs.
items.use_it_for:
- **Reasonable force (LEPRA s 231):** what excessive force looks like, and the limits of accountability when the remedy is internal discipline. Compare *R v White* [2025] NSWSC 243 (Clare Nowland), where an officer was prosecuted.
- **Accountability bodies:** the Coroner finds facts and recommends; it cannot punish.
items.caution: Written from media summaries of the findings; quote the Coroner's words from the findings themselves before using them in an exam answer. The cause of death was not formally attributed to the Taser alone.

sections.What the Coroner found (14 November 2012:
- The actions of some officers were **reckless, careless, dangerous and excessively forceful**, and showed little understanding of the safe use of Tasers or OC spray; training was inadequate.

- The **NSW Ombudsman** reviewed Taser use (2012) and recommended clearer rules, including on repeated and drive-stun use.

items.citation: Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody, Report of the Inquiry into the Death of David John Gundy (Commissioner J H Wootten QC, 1991)
items.significance: A man shot dead by police in his bedroom during a dawn raid for someone else; the Commission condemned how the search warrant was obtained and executed and the failure to announce who police were.
items.lead: On 27 April 1989 members of the Special Weapons and Operations Section raided a house in Marrickville before dawn, looking for John Porter, who was wanted for shooting police officers. items.title: Tajjour v New South Wales [2014] HCA 35: the consorting offence upheld
items.citation: [2014] HCA 35 (8 October 2014)
items.significance: The consorting offence in Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s 93X burdens the implied freedom of political communication but is valid, because it is reasonably appropriate and adapted to preventing organised crime.
items.lead: **Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s 93X** (2012) makes it an offence to *habitually consort* with convicted offenders after an official police warning (maximum 3 years). Three people charged with consorting challenged the law in the High Court.
items.use_it_for:
- **Police powers and the balance of rights:** a preventive power (no proven offence) upheld as proportionate. Contrast *Lees* and *Jarrett* (2025–26), where protest powers failed the same test.
- **Rule of law:** the courts test Parliament's laws against the Constitution; here the law survived.
items.caution: The case upholds the law; the criticism is about how police use the discretion to warn and charge, which is the Ombudsman's point, not the Court's.

sections.Held:
- The offence **burdens the implied freedom of political communication**, because consorting can include political association, but the burden is justified: the law's purpose, preventing or impeding organised crime, is legitimate, and the offence is reasonably appropriate and adapted to it. The law is **valid**.
- The Court rejected the argument that the Constitution contains a free-standing freedom of association.
- The warning requirement and the defences (family, work, education, legal advice, health) were part of what made the burden proportionate.
sections.What happened next: The NSW Ombudsman's review (2016) found the offence was used heavily against **Aboriginal people and young people**, often for minor offending, and recommended changes; Parliament added further defences. The 2026 organised crime reforms added interim serious crime prevention orders alongside consorting.

items.title: The Wee Waa mass DNA screening (2000)
items.citation: NSW Police voluntary DNA screening of about 600 men in Wee Waa, April 2000; Crimes (Forensic Procedures) Act 2000 (NSW)
items.significance: Every man in a small town was asked to volunteer DNA after an elderly woman was raped; the offender confessed before his sample was analysed, raising privacy and presumption-of-innocence concerns.
items.lead: In January 1999 a 91-year-old woman, Rita Knight, was raped and assaulted in her home in Wee Waa, in north-west NSW. In **April 2000** police asked every man in the town aged 18 to 45 (about 600) to give a voluntary mouth swab for DNA comparison: Australia's first mass DNA screening.
items.use_it_for: - **Use of technology / DNA evidence:** the power of DNA and the rights it engages. Pair with *Farah Jama* (contamination) and *R v White* (2005) (covert collection).
items.caution: Figures (about 600 men; the sentence) are from media reports of the time; verify before quoting.

sections.What happened:
- Most men volunteered; those who declined were reported to feel under suspicion in a small town.
- **Stephen Boney**, 44, gave a sample and confessed about a week later, before his sample had been analysed. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 18 years.
- The **Crimes (Forensic Procedures) Act 2000 (NSW)** commenced soon after, regulating consent, orders by senior police and magistrates, and the destruction of samples from volunteers.
sections.Issues raised:
- **Privacy and the presumption of innocence:** treating a whole population as suspects, with social pressure making 'voluntary' consent questionable.
- **Effectiveness:** the screening produced a confession, arguably through pressure rather than science, at considerable cost.
- **Retention:** what happens to the DNA of the hundreds of men who were not suspects.

items.title: Aboriginal children far less likely to be diverted from court — BOCSAR Crime and Justice Bulletin 282 (October 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of M Zappia, Examining disparities in police diversion between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal children in NSW, Crime and Justice Bulletin No 282 (BOCSAR, October 2026; released 10 November 2026); Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) ss 7, 8, 13–14
items.significance: Even where diversion was legally available, police sent 54% of Aboriginal children's matters to court against 24% of others. About 8 points of the 30-point gap cannot be explained by legal factors.
items.document: Crime/Media/Crime - BOCSAR Police Diversion Disparities Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
BOCSAR analysed **56,742** police events involving **23,605** children. **68%** of Aboriginal children's events went to court
against **38%** of non-Aboriginal children's; among events eligible for YOA diversion the figures were **54%** and **24%**.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.5.5 / crime.2.1** — police discretion under the YOA and whether it is applied fairly.
- **Effectiveness** — diversion is the law's main tool for keeping children out of court; unequal use undermines it.
items.caution: A **class summary of a statistical bulletin**: the findings are associations, not proof of bias or its cause.

sections.How police dealt with eligible matters:
| | Aboriginal children | Non-Aboriginal children |
|---|---|---|
| Sent to court | 54% | 24% |
| Warned | 10% | 22% |
| Cautioned | 30% | 48% |
| On bail when proceeded against | About 30% | About 13% |
| First formal contact sent to court | 10% | 5% |

Of the **30-point** gap, about 22 points link to offence type (5), bail status (5) and prior contact (the rest); about
**8 points are unexplained** (18–22 explained under other weightings). The gap grows from 15 points at ages 10–11 to 36 at 17,
because each formal contact makes later diversion less likely.
sections.The diversion ladder:
Section 7 says the least restrictive suitable option should be used and Aboriginal over-representation addressed through
diversion. Excluded offences (s 8) go to court; warnings suit non-violent summary offences; cautions needed an admission
(from 1 July 2026 a non-denial statement suffices, with a three-cautions-in-three-years limit); conferences for more serious
eligible offending.

- **History**: BOCSAR found 64.8% of eligible Indigenous young people diverted against 85.1% of others (2013); the youth
  diversion rate fell from 51.3% to 46.8% (2024); the Productivity Commission says NSW is worsening on Closing the Gap Target 11.
sections.In the media (AAP, 10 November 2026):
AAP's report ("Racism blamed for Indigenous youth police treatment") adds Aboriginal Legal Service and ministerial views; no NSW
Police response was included. A [second class summary, built on the AAP report](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1B3EVBfgdwTPmw1RBuGuCfWOuI458iE8U/view) notes
the YOA's objects (s 3(d)) and that about **72%** of the gap is linked to recorded factors — leaving the unexplained 8 points as a
question of equality before the law.

- **crime.5.5 / crime.2.1** — police discretion under the YOA and whether it is applied fairly.
- **Effectiveness** — diversion is the law's main tool for keeping children out of court; unequal use undermines it.

items.title: Black v R; Trautsch v R [2026] NSWCCA 185 — former police officers' sentences cut for errors with aggravating factors
items.short: Black v R; Trautsch v R
items.citation: [2026] NSWCCA 185 (Dhanji, McNaughton and Coleman JJ, 9 November 2026)
items.significance: Two former officers who assaulted a vulnerable woman and used OC spray won sentence appeals: gratuitous cruelty could not aggravate the assaults, and trust and authority were double counted.
items.document: Cases/Crime/Black v R; Trautsch v R [2026] NSWCCA 185 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Black v R; Trautsch v R [2026] NSWCCA 185 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
On 22 January 2023 two on-duty NSW police officers attended a woman in distress; they assaulted her and used OC spray, and
Black also sent protected video. Both pleaded guilty (10% discount) to common assault and unauthorised use of a prohibited
weapon. The District Court sentenced Black to **5 years 9 months** and Trautsch to **5 years 6 months** (8 August 2025).
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.3 / crime.4.5** — statutory aggravating factors and appeals against sentence.
- **Moral and ethical standards** — police who abuse their position are still sentenced on correct principles.
items.caution:
Manifest excess was not decided, and Trautsch's hospital evidence was not admitted. Coleman J's reasons are at [142], not
[147] as the judgment header says.

sections.The three questions:
| Issue | Held |
|---|---|
| Can an assault be aggravated by **gratuitous cruelty** (s 21A(2)(f))? | Not the assaults here; the factor needs pain as an end in itself |
| Was it an error to find both **abuse of trust and abuse of authority** (s 21A(2)(k))? | Yes — counting both without explanation risked double weight |
| What sentences on resentencing? | Black **3 years 2 months** (non-parole 2 years 1 month); Trautsch **3 years** (non-parole 2 years) |

items.lead:
A man in his 20s admitted **seven** offences against his mother across two incidents (November 2025 and February 2026),

magistrate called DV "a scourge in our society". He received a **one-year intensive correction order** with 50 hours' community

sections.Sentencing a DV offender in NSW:
| Step | Rule |
|---|---|
| A DV offence | Personal violence against a relative (CDPVA s 11; parents and children are relatives) |

items.title: Northern Rivers flood pod villages wind down as the 2027 end nears (NSW Government, 9 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of a NSW ministerial media release (Janelle Saffin and Rose Jackson), 9 November 2026; NSW Audit Office report (2024); State Environmental Planning Policy (Housing) 2021 (NSW)
items.significance: The state built disaster shelter after the 2022 floods; turning pods into permanent homes is harder. The Audit Office found no exit plan, and no flood-free lots had been delivered by March 2026.
items.document: Shelter/Evidence Sheets/Shelter - Northern Rivers Temporary Housing Villages Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
After the 2022 floods the government built **546** dwellings across **11** villages; **1,021** people lived in them in July 2023.
Five closed in 2025. The remaining six were extended to December 2026; the 9 November release sets a different outcome for each.

| Village | After 9 November 2026 |
|---|---|
| Ballina, Mullumbimby | Homes NSW keeps managing for 12 more months |
| Brunswick Heads | Offered to Byron Shire Council, which sought a community housing provider |
| Coraki | Offered to Richmond Valley Council; 56 pods considered for worker accommodation |
| Lismore, Wardell | Close early 2027; decommissioned for future housing |
items.use_it_for:
- **shel.2.8 / shel.1.3** — government as a direct provider of shelter after a disaster, and the limits of that role.
- **shel.3.3** — the government pledges no one will be left homeless; the Auditor-General warned of no exit strategy.
items.caution: A **government promotional release**: no resident numbers, outcome data or resident, council or advocate voices.

sections.The pathway:
Emergency accommodation (peaking at 1,440 people in April 2022) → a temporary village under an occupancy agreement → an
income-tested licence fee from late 2024 → individual support and up to **$10,000** to move on → a permanent home. Villages must
be demobilised within five years under the Housing SEPP. **0 of 4,382** planned flood-free homes or lots had been delivered by
31 March 2026; about 270 residents had moved to longer-term housing by August 2024.

items.title: Younger borrowers risk being locked in "mortgage prison" (SMH, 9 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Clancy Yeates, The Sydney Morning Herald, 9 November 2026, drawing on Equifax and Canstar data; National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009 (Cth) ss 128–133; National Credit Code s 72; APRA APS 220 serviceability buffer
items.significance: Laws meant to stop unaffordable lending can also trap existing borrowers: after five 2026 rate rises and falling prices, recent buyers who fail a new lender's test cannot switch.
items.document: Shelter/Evidence Sheets/Shelter - Mortgage Prison and Refinancing Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
The RBA's fifth 2026 rise (3 November) took the cash rate to **4.85%**, the highest since 2008. Refinancing to a new lender by
26–35-year-olds fell **14.2%** in the year to September, while it rose for over-55s. National home values are down **6.7%** from
the March 2026 peak, and a record **5.8%** of new loans were approved as serviceability exceptions (June quarter).

|---|---|---|

items.title: Peers v Eastern Health [2026] FCA 1677 — a dismissed anaesthetist's s 109 challenge to a Victorian pandemic law fails
items.citation: [2026] FCA 1677 (McEvoy J, 10 November 2026)
items.significance: A former anaesthetist asked the Federal Court to declare a Victorian pandemic law inoperative under s 109. The Court had jurisdiction but found no inconsistency, no utility in declarations and no standing.
core_labels: The division of powers between federal, state and territory governments
The role, jurisdiction and hierarchy of courts in NSW and Australia
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Peers v Eastern Health [2026] FCA 1677 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
Dismissed by Eastern Health in 2022 for misconduct linked to her vaccination status, the applicant (self-represented) sought
declarations that s 165AI of Victoria's *Public Health and Wellbeing Act* was inconsistent with the *Fair Work Act* and so
**inoperative under s 109** of the Constitution. The matter came to the Federal Court from the High Court.
items.use_it_for:

  and courts testing a State Act against a Commonwealth Act (inv.4.5, inv.5.4).
items.caution:
Year 11 only: a federalism case, not a human rights case — no rights instrument is discussed. The file gives two dates for the
end of later directions.

sections.The questions:

|---|---|
| Jurisdiction (ss 71, 77) | Yes, the Federal Court had jurisdiction |
| Inconsistency under s 109 | None — the State and Commonwealth laws can operate together |
| Utility of declarations | None |
| Standing | No |

All claims failed; she was ordered to pay **costs**.
